newsitem.title: BELARUS: Russia criticises Belarus over press freedom.
newsitem.headline: Russia criticises Belarus over press freedom.

text.p: Belarussian relations with Moscow and Washington were looking strained on Tuesday as hardline President Alexander Lukashenko prepared to visit Russian President Boris Yeltsin and sign a deal on a union.

Just a week before Lukashenko's trip to Russia, Minsk has drawn harsh criticism from the U.S. State Department which said on Monday that it "deplored" the expulsion of the first secretary of its embassy in Belarus.
The Kremlin, rarely openly critical of its small western "cousin", criticised Belarus on Tuesday for cracking down on Russian journalists working there.

"The very fact that Russian television channels have been denied the right to send information material from Minsk prompts deep concern in the Kremlin," spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing in Moscow.
"We have the right to expect that the principles of freedom of information will be restored in full," he added.

Belarus authorities began cracking down on foreign television broadcasters on Sunday, stopping Russian journalists from entering the main television centre. It extended the restriction to other foreign broadcasters on Monday.
Lukashenko and Yeltsin agreed last April 2 to form a "commonwealth" of two states, and a new deal is due to be signed at a meeting next week marking the anniversary.
The agreement is expected to move towards closer economic union, but it is unclear how far it will go towards full merger.
Yeltsin has mooted union as a possibility while Lukashenko stresses any merger must be one between two sovereign states.
Opposition forces in Minsk plan to mark the meeting with big protests which have turned violent in the past, particularly last Sunday when a nationalist rally erupted in clashes.
Moscow's criticism came on the heels of a serious worsening in Belarus-U.S. relations, strained since Belarussian armed forces shot down a sports balloon in 1995 killing two American pilots.
A spokeswoman for the U.S. embassy said first secretary Serzh Alexandrov, of Belarussian origin, had left the country late on Monday following an expulsion order on Sunday.
The decision to expel him sparked an outcry from the State Department in Washington which said it deplored the move.
Lukashenko took a step back in the row on Monday, saying he wanted to strengthen relations with Washington.

"We don't want people to say that there was an anti-American campaign in Belarus," Lukashenko was quoted by state television as saying during a meeting with the newly-appointed Belarussian ambassador to the United States, Valery Tsepkalo.
Alexandrov was arrested at Sunday's rally and accused of "provocative" actions but the embassy said he was carrying out his normal diplomatic duties by observing a political rally.
Last week Washington said it had cut off $40 million in aid to the country of 10 million because of its human rights record.
U.S. officials have also criticised Belarussian authorities for media restrictions, which have sharpened in recent days.
Alexander Stupnikov, a reporter for Russia's NTV channel, had his accreditation withdrawn for "systematic distortion of information about our country", state television said on Monday.
Reporters who attended a news conference on Tuesday due to be held by Lukashenko's press spokesman waited 40 minutes to be told he was "probably meeting the president".
Journalists handed in a protest note at the Foreign Ministry about the move against Stupnikov, an Israeli citizen.
The government announced on Monday it was banning the import and export of "all audio, video and text material which could damage the political or economic interests of the country".
